title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers operating and evolving Redwood's inference serving runtime.

Goals & scope

- Provide a single reference for architecture decisions that affect performance, latency, and cost.
- Describe kernel scheduling and affinity policies used across GPU fleets.
- Define profiling procedures and required metrics for performance triage.
- Specify benchmarking suite configuration and CI thresholds.
- Surface current known issues, mitigations, and release highlights.
- Provide on-call runbooks for common runtime incidents.

Audience

- Serving runtime engineers, infra SREs, performance engineers, and platform owners.

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

High-level components:

- Frontend (API layer): REST/GRPC ingress, request validation, routing.
- Router & policy engine: routes requests by latency, cost, region, and model compatibility.
- Serving runtime (executor): handles model loading, KV cache management, batching, token generation loops.
- Kernel selection & compilation layer: compiles/chooses kernels per model and sequence profile; stores optimized kernels in artifact cache.
- Storage layers: model artifact store, KV cache (in-RAM + optional Redis backing), persistent logs.
- Telemetry pipeline: traces, metrics (Prometheus), and structured logs sent to observability systems.

Key principles:

- Optimize for tail latency (p95/p99) while maintaining high token throughput.
- Automatic batching with latency SLO-aware limits.
- KV prefix caching for hot contexts to reduce compute.
- Fallbacks to compatible model variants on resource constraints.

2) Kernel scheduling and GPU affinity

Scheduling goals:

- Maximize GPU utilization for high-throughput workloads without violating latency SLOs.
- Avoid cross-process interference by isolating long-running generation from short-latency requests when needed.

Scheduling concepts and policies:

- Worker pools: separate pools for low-latency (interactive) and high-throughput (bulk) workloads. Pools are tagged with QoS (latency, throughput, batchable).
- Slot allocation: each GPU is partitioned into N slots (logical worker slots). Slots are assigned based on request QoS and model memory footprint.
- Preemption: low-latency slots can preempt batchable jobs using checkpointed KV cache to resume when capacity returns.
- NUMA awareness: placement considers CPU-GPU NUMA affinity to reduce PCIe/NVLink cross hops for host-side preprocessing.
- CUDA stream & SM scheduling: runtime uses per-request CUDA streams and prioritizes low-latency streams where supported.
- Kernel packing: small kernels are coalesced where safe to increase SM occupancy.

Affinity and placement rules:

1. Prefer local GPU where model and KV cache are resident.
2. If local GPU capacity exhausted, attempt intra-node migration to idle slot before cross-node routing.
3. Avoid colocating multiple high-memory models on same GPU to prevent OOM.

3) Profiling playbook

When to profile:

- Regressions in p95/p99 latency after deploy.
- Unexpected GPU OOMs or memory fragmentation.
- Lower-than-expected tokens/sec for a target model.
- High GPU SM idle time despite queued work.

Required tools:

- NVIDIA Nsight Systems & Nsight Compute (for deep kernel-level sampling).
- nvidia-smi for quick health checks (GPU utilization, memory).
- PyTorch profiler / torch.profiler (for tracing autograd and operator time).
- CUPTI-based sampling if available for kernel timelines.
- Runtime internal tracing (span IDs, per-request metrics, KV cache hit rates).

Profiling checklist (step-by-step):

1. Reproduce on staging with production-like load.
2. Capture high-level metrics (Prometheus): request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, queue depth, KV cache hit rate, GPU util, memory used.
3. If GPU util < 40% with high queue depth, collect Nsight Systems timeline for ~60s to inspect kernel launch gaps.
4. Use Nsight Compute on the slow kernels to inspect SM occupancy, memory bound vs compute bound metrics, and register usage.
5. Correlate kernel timelines with runtime traces to identify host-side stalls (serialization, lock contention, memcpy).
6. Validate batch sizes and batching timeouts; check whether dynamic batching backpressure is operating correctly.
7. Check for frequent CUDA context switches or inter-process preemption events.
8. If OOMs observed, collect per-process memory maps and model allocator stats.
9. Produce a short findings summary with suggested remediation and a JIRA ticket reference.

Common profiling anti-patterns and fixes:

- High CPU serialization on tokenization path: move tokenization to worker threads pinned to same NUMA node as GPU.
- Low SM occupancy: enable kernel fusion/packing or bump batch sizes for throughput workloads.
- Frequent small kernel launches: enable micro-batching or combine kernels in fused ops.
- Memory fragmentation on long-running GPU processes: prefer model reloads on a schedule or use memory compaction strategies.

4) Benchmarking suite (configuration and CI)

Benchmarking goals:

- Continuous measurement of per-model latency and throughput across representative workloads.
- Detect regressions in token generation speed and latency SLOs caused by kernel or runtime changes.

Workloads:

- InteractiveShort: conversational prompts, median seq_len 32, latency-sensitive (p95 target 150ms).
- StdCompletion: completions, seq_len 128, balanced throughput.
- LongGeneration: seq_len 1024+, throughput-oriented.
- EmbeddingsBatch: batched embedding workloads for large-batch throughput.

Sample benchmark config (YAML):

benchmarks:
  - name: interactive-short
    model: redwood-open-3b
    concurrency: 64
    batch_policy: latency
    prompt_distribution: conversational
    seq_len: 32
    targets:
      p95_latency_ms: 150
      tokens_per_sec: 30000

CI integration:

- Benchmarks run nightly on a staging fleet that mirrors production HW (same GPU types and kernel caches).
- Pull requests touching runtime, kernel selection, or scheduler must include a micro-benchmark run. Failure to meet thresholds blocks merge.
- Historical results stored for trend analysis; alerts created on regression >5% for tokens/sec or >10% for p95 latency.

Bench report artifacts to collect:

- Raw traces (nsight sys), per-request traces, Prometheus metrics, and summarized CSV with p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and memory usage.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)

- 2027-02-28 (v3.8.1): Improved kernel packing for small-matrix GEMMs; average tokens/sec +8% for 3B models. Added preemption-safe KV checkpointing.
- 2026-12-15 (v3.7.0): Introduced NUMA-aware placement and per-pool CUDA stream prioritization.
- 2026-09-10 (v3.6.2): Fixed a regression causing memory leak in async tokenizer pool.

6) Known issues and mitigations

- Issue: Occasional p99 spikes when KV cache cold-starts after model migration.
  - Mitigation: Warm-up requests on new hosts; async prefetch of common prefixes.
- Issue: GPU memory fragmentation on very long-lived worker processes.
  - Mitigation: Periodic worker process restart (configurable window), use of pooled allocators with compaction.
- Issue: Cross-node routing increases tail latency for latency-sensitive requests.
  - Mitigation: Prefer intra-node migration; increase local capacity for low-latency pool and configure fallback model variants with lower memory.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook: High p95/p99 latency

1. Verify external causes: spike in request rate or bad prompt distribution.
2. Check Prometheus dashboards for queue depth, batch sizes, tokens/sec, KV cache hit rate.
3. If queue depth high and GPU util high: scale up dedicated pool or shift throughput traffic to batch pool.
4. If GPU util low but queue depth high: follow profiling checklist to identify kernel stalls.
5. If regression follows recent deploy: rollback to previous runtime image, create hotfix branch.

Runbook: GPU OOM

1. Identify process and model from logs (OOM stacktrace includes model id and process PID).
2. Reduce concurrency or evict less-priority models from host.
3. If fragmentation suspected: restart worker process on drained host.
4. Add quota/guardrails on model size per slot.

Runbook: Degraded tokens/sec for a model

1. Run micro-benchmark in staging matching problematic workload.
2. Compare kernel-level profiles to last-good baseline.
3. If kernel regression, consult kernel selection component to recompile or revert kernel artifact.

Escalation matrix

- Level 1: oncall runtime engineer (first 30 minutes)
- Level 2: performance team lead (30–90 minutes)
- Level 3: platform SRE and engineering manager (>90 minutes)

8) Team wiki & ownership

Appendix: SLO table

| SLO | Target | Owner | Notes |
|-----|--------|-------|-------|
| Interactive p95 latency | <= 150ms | serving-runtime | measured at gateway ingress |
| Completion p95 latency | <= 350ms | serving-runtime | seq_len 128 baseline |
| Throughput (tokens/sec) | >= baseline per model | performance | baseline published per-model in catalog |

Appendix: Example diagnostic commands

- Quick health check:
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used,name --format=csv -l 5
- Capture a 60s Nsight Systems trace on node (requires staging):
  - nsight-sys --trace=nvtx,cuda,osrt --output=trace.qsys --duration=60 --target-pid <pid>
- Fetch runtime traces for request id X:
  - curl -s "https://traces.internal.redwood/trace?request_id=<REQUEST_ID>" | jq
